title: How the Bangladesh Field Hospital Became the People's Health Centre
dek: In 1972 a surgeon who had left Britain for the war turned his bamboo field hospital into a rural health centre run on what the war had taught him about training.

story.event: Turning a wartime field hospital into a rural people's health centre at Savar
story.summary: During Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War, Zafrullah Chowdhury left surgical training in Britain and, with M. A. Mobin, set up a 480-bed field hospital near Agartala staffed largely by volunteers, many of them young women, trained on the job as paramedics. In 1972 officials objected to its name, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman chose 'Gonoshasthaya Kendra' (People's Health Centre); on donated and government land at Savar it became a rural health centre built around trained village paramedics, which Chowdhury led for 37 years.
paragraphs: In May 1971 Zafrullah Chowdhury, a young Bangladeshi doctor training as a surgeon in Britain, left before sitting his final examination. In London he had destroyed his Pakistani passport in Hyde Park, in protest, he said, at the army's killings at home. With the cardiac surgeon M. A. Mobin he reached Agartala, in India near the border, by late May. In the war sector commanded by Khaled Mosharraf they built the Bangladesh Field Hospital: 480 beds under bamboo and hay, for wounded freedom fighters and refugees.

There were doctors but no nurses. Chowdhury had hoped to bring nurses from England, but Tajuddin Ahmad, leading the government in exile, warned it could cause problems, Chowdhury recalled. So the doctors trained young volunteers, many of them women from the refugee camps, to work as paramedics and assist at operations. "I realised that it was not the amount of training that was important in this context but the access to training," he later said.

In April 1972, after independence, a concept paper called "Basic Health Care in Rural Area" was presented in Dhaka, and the founders set out to rebuild the hospital in the new country. Officials objected to its name, which made it sound like a state hospital. Chowdhury took his complaint to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, who asked for other names and chose one from Chowdhury's list: Gonoshasthaya Kendra, the People's Health Centre. It would have to work in education and agriculture as well as health, Mujib said. Three people gave five acres of family land at Savar, outside Dhaka, and Mujib arranged 23 more. The campus began on bare ground with a few health workers living in tents.

The wartime lesson became the method. Gonoshasthaya trained village women as paramedics who went from house to house on foot and later by bicycle, giving vaccinations, helping at births and teaching basic care; on 1 May 1977 a group of them cycled 25 miles from Savar to Dhaka despite loud objections from religious conservatives. It ran a health insurance scheme priced by what families could pay, and its experience shaped one of the working papers behind the Alma-Ata declaration on primary health care. Chowdhury led it for 37 years. He died in April 2023, aged 81, and was buried there.

quote.text: Now the man of perfect virtue, wishing to be established himself, seeks also to establish others; wishing to be enlarged himself, he seeks also to enlarge others.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius is answering a question about a man who confers benefits on all the people. Chowdhury left Britain without the final examination that would have established him as a surgeon, and spent the next fifty years establishing paramedics instead.

reflection: Emergencies force shortcuts, and most of them should be dropped once the pressure lifts. Chowdhury noticed which one should not. The war showed him that young women with little formal training could do skilled clinical work once someone let them in, and peace did not change that. It only removed the excuse for shutting the door again.

You have probably improvised through hard weeks too: handing a task to someone more junior because nobody else was free, or skipping a step that turned out not to matter. Some of those shortcuts were mistakes. One or two may have been better than the old way.
invitation: Think back to a recent stretch when you had to improvise. Name one thing that worked better than the usual way, and ask a colleague today whether it should become the usual way.

sources.title: Dr Zafrullah Chowdhury: The doctor with a heart of a warrior
sources.publisher: The Business Standard, Bangladesh (Sujan Sen Gupta, 12 April 2023)
sources.supports: FRCS training 1965-71 and leaving without the final exam; flight with Dr M. A. Mobin; field hospital at Melaghar with 480 beds, five Bangladeshi doctors and many untrained female volunteers; April 1972 concept paper 'Basic Health Care in Rural Area'; government objection to the name and Chowdhury's appeal to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, who chose 'Gonoshasthaya Kendra' from his list; 23 acres allocated by Mujib and five acres donated; project coordinator from 1972 for 37 years.

sources.title: Dr Zafrullah Chowdhury (1941-2023): One life, dedicated for the good of many
sources.publisher: The Business Standard, Bangladesh (Masum Billah, 13 April 2023)
sources.supports: Return from FRCS studies in London; first field hospital at Melaghar; the name 'Bangladesh Field Hospital' objected to in 1972 and the name Gonoshasthaya Kendra chosen with Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

sources.title: A fighter till the end
sources.publisher: The Daily Star, Bangladesh (Golam Mortoza, 13 April 2023)
sources.supports: Arrival in Agartala in late May 1971 with Dr Mobin; hospital in Sector 2 under Khaled Mosharraf, built of bamboo and hay with 480 beds; volunteers trained as paramedics; Chowdhury's account of tearing up his passport as a protest against the army's genocide; objection to the name, Mujib's choice of Gonoshasthaya Kendra and his remark that it should also work in education and agriculture; five acres donated at Savar by Zohra Begum, M. A. Rob and Dr Lutfor Rahman, and 23 acres from Mujib.

sources.title: The legacy of Zafrullah Chowdhury
sources.publisher: The Daily Star, Bangladesh (Golam Mortoza, 2 November 2018)
sources.supports: 480-bed Bangladesh Field Hospital founded with M. A. Mobin; volunteers trained as paramedics; 1972 attempt to rebuild the hospital in Bangladesh; objection to the name because it sounded like a government hospital; naming by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman; 5 donated plus 23 government-arranged acres at Savar.

sources.title: Tale of a field hospital for freedom fighters
sources.publisher: Prothom Alo English (interview by Abu Taib Ahmed, December 2017)
sources.supports: Chowdhury's own account: leaving his job in England; burning his Pakistani passport in Hyde Park; visiting Agartala with Dr Mobin in May 1971; plan to bring nurses from England opposed by Tajuddin Ahmad as likely to cause problems in the war; training young men and women as paramedics who ran the hospital.

sources.title: A revolutionary's journey
sources.publisher: The Daily Star, Bangladesh (Aasha Mehreen Amin, 11 April 2023)
sources.supports: No nurses at the field hospital; girls and young women from the refugee camps trained in first aid and to assist in operations; Chowdhury's remark that access to training mattered more than its amount; relocation to Savar as Gonoshasthaya Kendra; paramedics visiting homes on foot or by bicycle, vaccinating and assisting at deliveries.

sources.title: Radical pragmatist, champion of women, public-health advocate
sources.publisher: The Daily Star, Bangladesh (Steve Minkin, 26 April 2023)
sources.supports: The Savar campus beginning on barren land with a few health workers living in tents; women paramedics on bicycles despite loud objections from religious conservatives, and their 25-mile ride from Savar to Dhaka on 1 May 1977; health insurance priced by income and landholding.

sources.title: Dr Zafrullah Chowdhury - the indefatigable optimist (1941 to 2023)
sources.supports: Passed the primary FRCS but left before the final; 480-bed makeshift hospital at the Tripura border run by five doctors, a few medical students and many locally recruited women trained on the job as nurses and paramedics; relocation to Savar after the war; GK established 1972; its experience the basis of a working paper for the Alma-Ata Declaration; community insurance on ability to pay.

sources.title: Chowdhury, Zafrullah: 1985 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership
sources.supports: Leaving surgical training in London in 1971 to set up a field hospital whose patients came to include the rural poor; founding Gonoshasthaya Kendra at Savar as a charitable trust; village workers, two-thirds of them women, travelling by bicycle to vaccinate and treat common ailments; low-cost health insurance.

sources.title: Zafrullah Chowdhury / Gonoshasthaya Kendra (1992 Right Livelihood Award)
sources.supports: Gonoshasthaya Kendra founded in 1972 by Chowdhury and medical colleagues; paramedics as the backbone of its health care; insurance based on ability to pay.

sources.title: Dr Zafrullah laid to rest at Gonoshasthaya Kendra in Savar
sources.supports: Death in Dhaka at 81 and burial at Gonoshasthaya Kendra, Savar, on 14 April 2023.

research_notes: Place names differ: the hospital is placed at Melaghar (TBS), Bisramganj (Daily Star 2023), Agartala (Prothom Alo interview, Daily Star 2018) and 'the border of Tripura' (PHM); the story says it was in the Agartala area near the border, in Sector 2. Passport: Chowdhury told Prothom Alo he burned it in Hyde Park; the Daily Star quotes him on 'tearing up' it; the story says 'destroyed'. Founding date: TBS says the field hospital was converted into Gonoshasthaya Kendra 'on the last Sunday of 1972', after an April 1972 concept paper; other sources give only 1972; the story uses April for the paper and 1972 for the founding. The name: TBS says Mujib picked number two from Chowdhury's list; the Daily Star says each proposed three names and they chose together; the story says Mujib chose it from Chowdhury's list, which both support. Chowdhury's words to Mujib differ between translations and are paraphrased. Distance of Savar from Dhaka: about 40 km (Magsaysay) versus 'about 3 kilometres' (PHM, apparently an error); the story says only 'outside Dhaka'. Paramedics at the field hospital: the Prothom Alo interview says young men and women, PHM and the Daily Star (Amin) stress women; the story says 'many of them women'. Chowdhury's quotation on access to training appears in Aasha Mehreen Amin's Daily Star piece, from an earlier interview; it is the only source for that wording. Mujib's 'education and agriculture' remark is reported by Chowdhury via the Daily Star and is attributed to Mujib as reported. 'Fifty years' in the connection covers 1972 to his death in 2023. The Alma-Ata link is PHM's claim. The Bengali concept-paper title is given in TBS's English translation.
